stem.en: Quick recall before we start: on a velocity-time graph, what does the **slope** of the line tell you?

text.en: The acceleration — how fast the velocity itself is changing.

feedback.en: Right. Slope = rise ÷ run = Δv ÷ Δt — exactly the definition of acceleration.

text.en: The displacement — how far the object has travelled.

feedback.en: That's the AREA under the line, not its slope — a common mix-up between the two graph features. Slope measures a rate of change; area accumulates a quantity over time.

text.en: The object's speed at that instant.

feedback.en: Instantaneous speed is the graph's HEIGHT (its v-axis value) at that point, not its slope. Slope tells you how quickly that height is changing, not what the height currently is.

explanation.en: A velocity-time graph packs two different pieces of information into one picture: its height at any point gives the velocity there, and its slope gives the acceleration. This lesson leans on the slope reading constantly — every kinematic equation is really just this graph's geometry written out algebraically.

hints.en: Think about what 'slope' means on any graph: how much the y-value changes for each step along x.
Here y is velocity and x is time, so slope = Δvelocity ÷ Δtime — which quantity has exactly that definition?
